findings.title: Queue pool is destroyed on strategy close, so the consumer silently drops every message after a rebalance
findings.body: `SimpleQueueProcessingStrategy.close()` (and `terminate()`/`join()`) calls `self.queue_pool.shutdown()`, which sets `worker.shutdown = True` and calls `queue.shutdown()` on every queue. The `FixedQueuePool` is created once in `ResultsStrategyFactory.__init__` (result_consumer.py:133) and reused for every `create_with_partitions()` call. Arroyo invokes `close()`/`join()` on the strategy whenever partitions are revoked and then builds a new strategy on the next assignment. After the first rebalance the factory hands the new strategy the already-shut-down pool: the worker threads are dead and `work_queue.put()` raises `queue.ShutDown`, which is swallowed by the broad `except Exception` in `submit()` (line 317) where the offset is then marked complete and committed. The result is that every subsequent message is committed without ever being processed – permanent, silent data loss after any rebalance or partition reassignment. The pool (and its workers) needs to be created per assignment, or `close()` must not destroy state owned by the factory.

findings.title: OffsetTracker state is never reset between partition assignments
findings.body: The `FixedQueuePool` (and therefore its single `OffsetTracker`) is created once per factory and shared across all `create_with_partitions()` calls. `OffsetTracker.last_committed` and `all_offsets` therefore survive partition revocation. If a partition is revoked and later reassigned at a lower offset (offset reset, another consumer having made less progress, topic re-creation), `get_committable_offsets()` computes `start = max(last_committed + 1, min_offset)` and only reports an offset when `highest_committable > last_committed`, so no offset for that partition will ever be committed again and the consumer group silently stops advancing. In-flight work items belonging to the previous assignment also remain tracked and can be committed by the new strategy for partitions the consumer no longer owns.

findings.title: Offsets are committed from a background thread, outside arroyo's single-threaded strategy contract
findings.body: `_commit_loop` runs in its own daemon thread and calls `self.commit_function(committable)`, which is arroyo's `commit` callable wired to `StreamProcessor`/`KafkaConsumer`. Arroyo strategies are only ever called from the main consumer thread, and `KafkaConsumer.stage_offsets`/`commit_offsets` mutate consumer state (staged offsets, assignment/state checks) without locking. Committing from this thread races with `poll()`/rebalance callbacks on the main thread and can stage offsets for partitions that were just revoked, which arroyo rejects with `ConsumerError`, or corrupt the staged-offset bookkeeping. The exception is merely logged by the loop's `except Exception`, so the failure is invisible while offsets stop advancing.

findings.title: Failed work items have their offsets committed, contradicting the documented at-least-once guarantee
findings.body: In `OrderedQueueWorker.run`, any exception raised by `result_processor` is logged and the `finally` block still calls `offset_tracker.complete_offset(...)`, so the offset becomes committable. The same happens in `SimpleQueueProcessingStrategy.submit` (lines 317-325) when `grouping_fn` or the queue put fails. This makes processing at-most-once: a transient failure (DB blip, timeout) permanently drops the message, while the class docstring claims "No item is lost" and "Only commits offsets after successful processing". Either failures must block the commit / be routed to a DLQ, or the documented guarantee must be corrected.

findings.title: Queues are unbounded, so there is no backpressure and memory can grow without limit
findings.body: `queue.Queue()` is created with the default `maxsize=0` (unbounded) and `submit()` never raises `MessageRejected`, so arroyo will keep feeding messages as fast as it can poll regardless of how far behind the workers are. The docstring of `SimpleQueueProcessingStrategy` claims "Natural backpressure when queues fill up", which cannot happen. Each queued `WorkItem` additionally retains the full `Message[KafkaPayload]` (field `message`, never read anywhere), so a slow group pins both the decoded result and the raw Kafka payload in memory, and a backlogged consumer will OOM instead of applying backpressure.

findings.title: Shutdown sets the worker stop flag before queue.shutdown(immediate=False), so queued items are discarded instead of drained
findings.body: `FixedQueuePool.shutdown()` first sets `worker.shutdown = True` for every worker and only then calls `q.shutdown(immediate=False)`. Because the worker loop is `while not self.shutdown:`, each worker exits right after finishing the item it currently holds, so the "non-immediate" shutdown that is supposed to let queued items drain has no effect and all pending items are dropped. Combined with `close()` joining the commit thread before the pool shuts down, the final set of completed offsets may also never be committed, so a normal restart re-reads and re-processes more messages than necessary.

findings.title: Worker threads can block forever on queue.get(); shutdown failures are swallowed and leak threads
findings.body: `OrderedQueueWorker.run` uses a blocking `self.work_queue.get()` with no timeout, so the `self.shutdown` flag is only observed after an item arrives. Termination relies entirely on `queue.Queue.shutdown()` succeeding, but `FixedQueuePool.shutdown()` wraps that call in `except Exception: logger.exception(...)` (line 239). If it raises for any reason (e.g. the method is unavailable on the running Python version), every idle worker stays blocked in `get()`, `worker.join(timeout=5.0)` is executed sequentially for each worker, and shutdown stalls for 5s × num_queues (100s with the default of 20) before leaking the threads. Using `get(timeout=...)` would make the stop flag effective.

findings.title: test_thread_queue_parallel_error_handling asserts behaviour the implementation does not provide
findings.body: The test makes the result processor raise and then asserts `len(committed_offsets) == 0 or test_partition not in committed_offsets`, i.e. that a processing error prevents the offset from being committed. The implementation does the opposite: `OrderedQueueWorker.run` completes the offset in its `finally` block even when processing raises, so offsets 100 and 101 become committable. The assertion only holds because the polling loop breaks within ~0.3s while the commit thread ticks once per second; if the commit tick lands first the test fails. This test is both flaky and encodes a guarantee that does not exist – it should assert the real behaviour (or the behaviour should be fixed).

findings.title: Commit assertions race with the 1-second commit loop and will flake
findings.body: `test_offset_committing` and `test_handles_invalid_messages` wait for the first `commit_event` and then assert an exact final offset (104, resp. 101). The commit thread runs independently every second and commits whatever contiguous prefix is complete at that moment, so a tick that happens after only some offsets have been processed sets `commit_event` with a lower offset (e.g. 100 or 102); the subsequent `commit_event.wait()` returns immediately because the event is never cleared again and the equality assertion fails. The tests should poll until the expected offset is observed (or clear/re-wait) instead of asserting on the first commit.

findings.title: FilteredPayload messages are handled through the exception path, producing an error log per message
findings.body: `decode_payload` in the result consumer starts with `assert not isinstance(payload, FilteredPayload)`, which is outside its own try/except, so for every filtered message the `AssertionError` propagates into `submit()`'s broad `except Exception` and is reported via `logger.exception("Error submitting message to queue")`. Filtered payloads are a normal part of arroyo pipelines (e.g. when the stale-message DLQ wrapper is enabled), so this turns routine filtering into a flood of error-level exceptions with stack traces and relies on exceptions for ordinary control flow. `submit()` should check for `FilteredPayload` explicitly and complete the offset without logging.

findings.title: A gauge is emitted for every processed item on the hot path
findings.body: `OrderedQueueWorker.run` calls `metrics.gauge("remote_subscriptions.queue_worker.queue_depth", ...)` in the `finally` block of every single work item, with only an `identifier` tag so all 20 workers overwrite the same series. This adds per-message statsd overhead for a value that is already exported once per `poll()` by `SimpleQueueProcessingStrategy.poll` (`total_queued`), and the per-worker value is meaningless after aggregation. Emit it periodically rather than per item.
